item.title: Heparan sulfate sulfatases are essential for the patterning of human stem cell-derived midbrain dopaminergic neurons
item.dc:creator: Chiara Tremolanti
Carmen Abaurre
Yu-Chun Chien
Luke F. Gamon
Conor William Mitchell
Evelyne Gout
Eneritz Agirre
Guochang Lyu
item.description:
Authors: Chiara Tremolanti, Carmen Abaurre, Yu-Chun Chien, Luke F. Gamon, Conor William Mitchell, Evelyne Gout, Eneritz Agirre, Guochang Lyu, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11881
Abstract: Abstract Midbrain dopaminergic neurons (mDA) are selectively lost in Parkinson’s disease, driving sustained efforts to generate bona fide mDA neurons from human-induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) for replacement therapy. While morphogen gradients and transcription factors have been extensively studied, extracellular regulators remain largely overlooked. Here, we identify the heparan sulfate-modifying enzymes SULF1 and SULF2 as essential for establishing mDA neuron identity in vitro. Using CRISPR/Cas9-engineered iPSCs, we show that loss of SULF1/2 increases 6-O-sulfated heparan sulfate species and disrupts patterning both at the anteroposterior and dorsoventral axes in human iPSC-derived mDA cultures. Double-knockout cells thus fail to acquire ventral midbrain fates and instead adopt hindbrain, spinal cord and neural crest-like identities as revealed by single-nucleus RNA sequencing. Mechanistically, we partially explain the changed patterning to aberrant FGF signaling and demonstrate that FGF inhibition redirects cells toward midbrain fates, however without restoring ventral identity. These findings establish a critical role for SULF1/2 in mDA neuron in vitro differentiation and uncover a previously unrecognized layer of extracellular control over neural patterning.

item.title: The genetic and proteomic determinants of pediatric stature development and their link to adult height and type 2 diabetes
item.dc:creator: N. Fragoso-Bargas
AE Lupu
I. Campillo-Pereda
Y. Huang
J. Sundfjord
R. Karimi
T. Lind
JC Holm
item.description:
Authors: N. Fragoso-Bargas, AE Lupu, I. Campillo-Pereda, Y. Huang, J. Sundfjord, R. Karimi, T. Lind, JC Holm, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Stature is a key indicator of pediatric health, yet the molecular and metabolic architecture governing childhood growth remains incompletely defined. We conduct genome-wide association analyses of stature from birth to childhood (574,580 measurements; 72,704 Norwegian children) and integrate UK Biobank data (age 10 and adulthood). We uncover life-stage shifts in the genetics of stature, identifying previously not identified childhood-specific effects including variants near GLP1R with BMI-independent effects, and reveal three temporal clusters - Infancy and Childhood clusters enriched for endocrine and metabolic pathways, and a Lifetime growth cluster enriched for skeletal biology. Proteome analysis reveals that prepubertal height is associated with widespread changes in the circulation, identifying 106 height-associated proteins and linking IGF1, IGF2, and IGFBP3 levels to childhood-height polygenic scores. Mendelian randomization shows that reduced fetal growth and taller prepubertal height increase type 2 diabetes risk, independent of adult stature. These findings uncover developmental stage-specific genetic and proteomic influences on child-growth and links to adult metabolic health.

item.title: Foliar and floral frost damage reshape reproductive phenology with limited carry-over effects
item.dc:creator: Jianhong Lin
Nicolas Delpierre
Cyrille Rathgeber
Hai Ren
Jian-Guo Huang
Frank Berninger
Xiaobo Li
Qianqian Ma
item.description:
Authors: Jianhong Lin, Nicolas Delpierre, Cyrille Rathgeber, Hai Ren, Jian-Guo Huang, Frank Berninger, Xiaobo Li, Qianqian Ma
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Late spring frost is an intensifying climatic disturbance, yet how frost damage to different organs (leaves and flowers) reshapes reproductive phenology and generates carry-over effects remains unclear. Using 259,732 phenological observations across eight European woody species spanning 1950–2024, we show that foliar frost damage shortened the fruit development period (FDP; the interval from flowering to fruit maturity) by 1.6 days, driven by delayed flowering and advanced fruit maturity. Conversely, floral frost damage prolonged FDP by 1.3 days through delayed fruit maturity, with both effects strengthening under greater frost severity. Accounting for anomalously warm conditions in the frost year substantially reduced the estimated delays in flowering and subsequent-year phenology, indicating that neglecting climatic context leads to overestimation of frost effects. These findings reveal organ-specific pathways through which frost damage reshapes reproductive phenology while generating limited carry-over effects, refining current understanding of phenological responses under climate change.

item.title: Episodic memory consolidation by reactivation of human concept neurons during sleep reflects contents, not sequence of events
item.dc:creator: J. Niediek
T. P. Reber
M. Bausch
F. Schwimmbeck
H. Gast
V. A. Coenen
J. Boström

item.description:
Authors: J. Niediek, T. P. Reber, M. Bausch, F. Schwimmbeck, H. Gast, V. A. Coenen, J. Boström, C. E. Elger, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11880
Abstract: Abstract How do our brains manage to store our everyday experiences into memory? Neurons in the human temporal lobe that respond to the concept of an individual person or object have been shown to provide the semantic building blocks for episodic memory. Recording from 1415 neurons in neurosurgical patients who learned a story involving specific concepts, we found reactivation of neurons representing these concepts during slow-wave sleep after learning. Concept neurons were conjointly reactivated, particularly during sharp-wave ripples, with time lags suitable for synaptic modification. However, the temporal sequence of reactivation did not reflect the sequence of concepts in the learned story. Unlike rodent place cells, which can acquire preferred firing locations during exploration of new environments according to their pre-existing preferred sequence of activation, human concept neurons are tuned to specific semantic contents before learning starts. Consequently, pre-existing firing sequences correlate with consecutive place fields in rodents, but not with sequences of events in human experience. Thus, in contrast to reactivation of rodent place cells, reactivation of human concept cells does not reflect sequences of events in human experience.

item.title: Benzoxaboroles target CPSF3 for degradation through a SUMO-dependent pathway in trypanosomes
item.dc:creator: Ning Zhang
Farnaz Zahedifard
Abdul Samad
Simone Altmann
Melanie Ridgway
Richard J. Wall
Michele Tinti

item.description:
Authors: Ning Zhang, Farnaz Zahedifard, Abdul Samad, Simone Altmann, Melanie Ridgway, Richard J. Wall, Michele Tinti, Eric C. Schirmer, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Benzoxaboroles (BoBs) such as acoziborole feature a boron-heterocyclic core and are an important innovation in the development of drugs against a range of pathogens and other pathologies. A broad pharmacological spectrum is associated with chemically diverse BoB derivatives, including multiple modes-of-action (MoA) and molecular targets. However, a consensus MoA for BoBs targeting evolutionarily diverse protozoan pathogens has emerged, with identification of CPSF3 in the CPSF complex as a target in both apicomplexan and kinetoplastida parasites. Here, using comprehensive genetic screens in Trypanosoma brucei , we establish a functional connection between the boron-heterocyclic scaffold shared by all BoBs and protein sumoylation genes. We observe a rapid, transient increase in global protein sumoylation following BoB exposure. While we do not observe direct CPSF3 sumoylation, we find that acoziborole and other BoBs rapidly and specifically destabilise CPSF3 in a SUMO- and proteasome-dependent manner.

item.title: Chronically stable, frequency-selective auditory brainstem stimulation via ultra-flexible penetrating electrode arrays
item.dc:creator: Jinxi Pan
Bodi Liu
Zeyu Wang
Guangyuan Chen
Chengyao Wang
Ying Chen
Huan Jia
Zhaoyan Wang
item.description:
Authors: Jinxi Pan, Bodi Liu, Zeyu Wang, Guangyuan Chen, Chengyao Wang, Ying Chen, Huan Jia, Zhaoyan Wang, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The auditory brainstem implant (ABI) targeting the cochlear nucleus (CN) can restore hearing in patients ineligible for cochlear implants. However, conventional ABI using surface electrode array yields highly variable outcomes, from poor to moderate, due to limited spatial resolution and restricted tonotopic access. Here, we developed a penetrating ABI based on a high-density, ultra-flexible implantable neural electrode array (uFINE). In normal-hearing rats, uFINE mapped frequency tuning from 0.5 to 32 kHz in CN and the inferior colliculus (IC). Selective CN stimulation via uFINE evoked IC responses closely matching acoustic tonotopy, with IC tuning widths comparable to tone-evoked responses, and these remained stable for over 136 days, with minimal gliosis observed. Daily sequential CN–IC microstimulation progressively shifted the location of the CN-evoked IC response peak toward the targeted IC stimulation site, consistent with use-dependent plasticity. Together, these findings demonstrate that uFINE enables high-resolution, tonotopically precise, and long-term stable CN stimulation across a broad frequency range with minimal tissue disruption, highlighting its potential to enhance ABI-mediated hearing restoration.

item.title: Desmin filaments extend along actin filaments within the mouse skeletal muscle sarcomere
item.dc:creator: Sunu Joseph
Joon-Hyuk Ko
Nitsan Dahan
Tali Dadosh
Hana K. Pak
Jonathan A. Kirk
Wonho Jhe
Shenhav Shemer
item.description:
Authors: Sunu Joseph, Joon-Hyuk Ko, Nitsan Dahan, Tali Dadosh, Hana K. Pak, Jonathan A. Kirk, Wonho Jhe, Shenhav Shemer
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Although desmin intermediate filaments are critical for muscle architecture and homeostasis, their spatial 3D organization remains elusive. Their known localization to sarcomeric Z-lines delimits the periodic array of actin and myosin filaments. Here, using d STORM and SIM sub-diffraction resolution microscopy, we resolve the spatial 3D organization of desmin filaments within mouse skeletal muscle, and reveal they are not confined to Z-lines. Our reconstruction reveals that desmin intermediate filaments extend from Z-lines into the sarcomere interior, where they align with actin filaments. Functional assays show that disrupting desmin filament assembly in normal male mouse muscle using a dominant negative inhibitor of desmin selectively reduces active tension at longer sarcomere lengths, indicating a role for desmin in sarcomere mechanics. These findings expand the structural model of the muscle sarcomere and support a role for desmin in force production.

item.title: A highly distorted benzenium cation
item.dc:creator: Baojing Tian
Jiaofan Chang
Qi Sun
Qi Zhang
Shaowen Zhang
He Huang
Xudong Xu
Zongyao Sun
item.description:
Authors: Baojing Tian, Jiaofan Chang, Qi Sun, Qi Zhang, Shaowen Zhang, He Huang, Xudong Xu, Zongyao Sun, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract In contrast to the well-explored peripheral functionalization of benzene, its skeletal alteration remains underdeveloped. Here, we report a highly distorted benzenium cation, 2,3-dihydroxy-1,4,6-triamino-5-nitrobenzenium (TANBC + ), featuring a ring twist angle of 35.91° and a ring C-C bond length of 1.540 Å, both rank the highest among all benzenium cations. Such pronounced structural distortions endow TANBC + with unique electronic properties, including a highly positive electrostatic charge on the warped carbon, weak aromaticity, and a low ring bond dissociation energy. Consequently, instead of undergoing peripheral functionalization like typical benzenium cations, TANBC + participates in three distinct benzene ring reconstruction pathways or remains inert under standard electrophilic substitution conditions. Moreover, despite its distorted structure, TANBC + exhibits excellent ambient stability, stabilized by extensive hydrogen bonding, and can be synthesized readily without harsh conditions usually required for conventional benzenium cations. This work not only introduces a new strategy for benzene reconstruction but also redefines the role of benzenium cations from mediators of peripheral functionalization to promoters of skeletal alteration, thereby advancing the fundamental chemistry of benzene.

item.title: Greenhouse gas responses to coastal wetland land use change vary by ecosystem and conversion pathway
item.dc:creator: Zihao Wang
Feifei Yan
Can Wang
Jingyu Sun
Mingzhi Liu
Xianbiao Lin
item.description:
Authors: Zihao Wang, Feifei Yan, Can Wang, Jingyu Sun, Mingzhi Liu, Xianbiao Lin
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Land-use and land-cover change (LULCC) is altering greenhouse gas (GHG) dynamics in coastal wetlands, yet how these responses vary among ecosystems and conversion pathways remains uncertain. Here, we synthesized 276 studies and applied multilevel meta-analysis to paired LULCC comparisons. GHG responses varied with pre-conversion wetland type, destination land use, hydrology, and soil carbon and nitrogen status. Pooled sustained-flux global warming potential (SGWP) was ‒122.41 ± 81.99 mg CO 2 e m ‒2 h ‒1 for natural coastal wetlands and 250.60 ± 101.06 for LULCC sites, corresponding to 0.17 ± 0.06 Gt CO 2 e of cumulative emissions over two decades. The descriptive SGWP contrast with pooled LULCC sites was larger for vegetated wetlands ( + 309.32%) than for tidal flats ( + 165.02%). Ecologically restored wetlands showed negative pooled SGWP ( − 33.03 ± 114.70 mg CO 2 e m ‒2 h ‒1 ), contrasting with the positive pooled LULCC estimate. Our results indicate that GHG responses to coastal wetland conversion are ecosystem- and pathway-specific, underscoring the importance of conserving vegetated wetlands and targeting restoration.

item.title: Visible light drives bright extreme-ultraviolet high harmonics
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Karst
Martin Gebhardt
Lucas Eisenbach
Philipp Gierschke
Themistoklis Sidiropoulos
Robert Klas
Jan Rothhardt

item.description:
Authors: Maximilian Karst, Martin Gebhardt, Lucas Eisenbach, Philipp Gierschke, Themistoklis Sidiropoulos, Robert Klas, Jan Rothhardt, Jens Limpert
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11879
Abstract: Abstract Coherent extreme-ultraviolet (XUV) light is a central tool in modern photon science, probing the electronic, chemical and structural properties of matter. High-harmonic generation can extend the reach of laser sources into this spectral range, but the achievable photon flux falls sharply as photon energy increases. We show experimentally and theoretically that plasma-core-induced self-guiding of a visible-wavelength driver in helium sustains high intensity and favorable phase matching over an extended propagation length. We achieve a conversion efficiency of up to 10 −6 in a single high-harmonic line and phase-matched emission extending to 100 eV. With less than 10 W of average power at 516 nm from a frequency-doubled ytterbium laser, we generate 1.8 × 10 11 photons s −1 within 2 % bandwidth at 13.5 nm (91.8 eV), exceeding previous reports by more than an order of magnitude. These results establish a power-scalable XUV platform for actinic metrology, spectroscopy and coherent imaging.

item.title: Accelerating high-throughput catalyst screening by direct generation of equilibrium adsorption structures
item.dc:creator: Songze Huo
Xiao-Ming Cao
item.description:
Authors: Songze Huo, Xiao-Ming Cao
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The adsorption energy serves as a crucial descriptor for the large-scale screening of catalysts. Nevertheless, the limited distribution of training data for the extensively utilised machine learning interatomic potential, predominantly sourced from near-equilibrium structures, results in unreliable adsorption structures and consequent adsorption energy predictions. In this context, we present DBCata, a deep generative model that integrates a periodic Brownian-bridge framework with an equivariant graph neural network to establish a low-dimensional transition manifold between unrelaxed and DFT-relaxed structures, without requiring explicit energy or force information. Upon training, DBCata effectively generates high-fidelity adsorption geometries, achieving an interatomic distance mean absolute error of 0.035 Å on the dataset from Catalysis-Hub, which is approximately 70% lower than that of the current state-of-the-art machine learning potential models. Moreover, the corresponding DFT accuracy can be improved within 0.1 eV in 94% of instances by identifying and refining anomalous predictions through a hybrid chemical-heuristic and self-supervised outlier detection approach. We demonstrate that DBCata enables accelerated high-throughput computational screening for alloy catalysts in the oxygen reduction reaction, highlighting the potential of DBCata as a powerful tool for catalyst design and optimisation.

item.title: Biosynthesis of iboga alkaloids
item.dc:creator: Moonyoung Kang
Mohamed Omar Kamileen
Yoko Nakamura
John P. Hamilton
Gyumin Kang
Bruno Huettel
Jens Wurlitzer
Sarah Heinicke
item.description:
Authors: Moonyoung Kang, Mohamed Omar Kamileen, Yoko Nakamura, John P. Hamilton, Gyumin Kang, Bruno Huettel, Jens Wurlitzer, Sarah Heinicke, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11878
Abstract: Abstract Tabernanthe iboga (iboga) is the source of voacangine, which is widely used as a semi-synthetic starting material for the anti-addiction agent ibogaine. Despite extensive investigation of voacangine biosynthesis, production of this compound cannot be reconstituted in a heterologous host, suggesting that one or more enzymes required for biosynthesis are missing. Additionally, T. iboga produces ibophyllidine, a pyrroloindole alkaloid that utilizes the same upstream precursor as voacangine, but is a member of a structurally distinct alkaloid class. Here we use bulk and single cell gene expression from leaf and root tissue to identify the unknown enzymes from these two pathways. We identify two additional enzymes that enable biosynthesis of voacangine in a heterologous host. The missing enzymes includes a pathogenesis-related (PR)10 family protein that likely catalyzes cyclization of a transient intermediate. Careful analysis of gene expression profiles in leaf and root also enabled the discovery of four additional enzymes that convert an upstream intermediate to ibophyllidine. This work reveals the chemical logic that generates two distinct alkaloid scaffolds in this important medicinal plant.

item.title: Mapping temperature using transmission Kikuchi diffraction
item.dc:creator: Yueyun Chen
Xin Yi Ling
Jared J. Lodico
Tristan P. O’Neill
B. C. Regan
Matthew Mecklenburg
item.description:
Authors: Yueyun Chen, Xin Yi Ling, Jared J. Lodico, Tristan P. O’Neill, B. C. Regan, Matthew Mecklenburg
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract As electronic devices are engineered at increasingly smaller length scales, new nanoscopic metrologies are needed. Measuring nanoscale temperatures and pressures is challenging as physical contact inevitably perturbs the system, and collecting far-field thermal radiation limits the spatial resolution. Kikuchi diffraction thermometry (KDTh), a non-contact scanning electron microscope (SEM) technique, can sensitively map nanoscale temperatures. Local lattice changes measured by Kikuchi pattern fitting enable translating volumetric strain to temperature via the material’s coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE). Measurements on Joule-heated graphite come from rastering a 5.5-nm electron probe across the sample, achieving a ~ 0.01% fractional precision and 2.2 K/ $$\sqrt{{{\rm{Hz}}}}$$ Hz temperature sensitivity. KDTh offers superior sensitivity by fitting the entire Kikuchi pattern, instead of a particular Kikuchi band or interband angle. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) techniques can achieve a similar precision, but electron-transparency limits their applications. KDTh can operate in both transmission and reflection modes to cost-effectively accommodate a variety of samples.

item.title: Deep ultraviolet gallium-oxide avalanche photodiodes reaching an impulse-response-derived gain-bandwidth record of 152 GHz
item.dc:creator: Dianmeng Dong
Jintao Fu
Hongda Ren
Qingyi Zhang
Tao Zhang
Xingsi Liu

item.description:
Authors: Dianmeng Dong, Jintao Fu, Hongda Ren, Qingyi Zhang, Tao Zhang, Xingsi Liu, Yilin Cao, Min Peng, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Solar-blind Ga 2 O 3 -based photodetectors, sensing deep ultraviolet (DUV) light (200–280 nm), offer unparalleled opportunities for secure non-line-of-sight optical communication. Yet their practical applications have been largely hindered by the relatively low gain-bandwidth product (GBP), due to the fundamental trade-off between response speed and photoelectric gain. Here, we report nanosecond-level-response solar-blind avalanche photodetectors based on β-Ga 2 O 3 /MgO/La 0.8 Ca 0.2 MnO 3 (LCMO) n-Barrier-p heterojunctions with high apparent gain over 2.6×10 6 , thereby achieving an impulse-response-derived record-breaking 152 GHz gain-bandwidth product — outpacing the state-of-the-art Ga 2 O 3 -based devices by 3 orders of magnitude. The MgO interlayer enables lattice matching and engineered conduction band offset to boost gain and suppress dark current, while the p-type LCMO layer introduces a large valence band offset and simultaneously establishes a hole-selective transport highway for ultrafast response. This work not only resolves the longstanding gain-bandwidth trade-off in DUV photodetection but also presents a universal band-engineering framework for next-generation optoelectronics.

item.title: Influenza A virus orchestrates ciliated cell fate and injury during the mucociliary damage repair cycle
item.dc:creator: Biying Xiao
Xuenan Zhao
Shiyong Guo
Mingyue Fan
Hui Zhang
Xiaojing Yang
Lulu Zhang
Yuting Li
item.description:
Authors: Biying Xiao, Xuenan Zhao, Shiyong Guo, Mingyue Fan, Hui Zhang, Xiaojing Yang, Lulu Zhang, Yuting Li, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Influenza A virus causes acute damage to airway epithelium, yet the damage–repair cycle and mechanisms underlying persistent mucociliary clearance (MCC) dysfunction long after viral clearance remain unclear. Here, using longitudinal in vivo quantitative micro-optical coherence tomography, we show that global MCC impairment persists for more than 14 days, marked by impaired ciliary activity and sustained mucus hypersecretion in male mice infected with the H1N1 influenza A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 (PR8) strain. Through lineage tracing and multi-omics analyses, we identify an immune-mediated transdifferentiation program in which IFN signaling activates the IDO1–AhR axis to drive ciliated-to-mucous cell fate transition and chronic muco-obstruction after H1N1 PR8 infection in a reconstructed human bronchial epithelium model. In parallel, we identify the viral M2 protein as a key driver of ciliary loss, suppressing the host TP73–FOXJ1–RFX3 regulatory axis and promoting proteasomal degradation of FOXJ1. Together, these findings uncover host- and virus-driven pathways that cooperatively impair airway epithelial homeostasis and sustain MCC failure beyond active infection, highlighting therapeutic targets for post-influenza muco-obstructive disease.

item.title: A global atlas of digital dermatology to map innovation and disparities
item.dc:creator: Fabian Gröger
Simone Lionetti
Philippe Gottfrois
Alvaro Gonzalez-Jimenez
Lea Habermacher
Maximilian Böhm
Sara Cerminara
item.description:
Authors: Fabian Gröger, Simone Lionetti, Philippe Gottfrois, Alvaro Gonzalez-Jimenez, Lea Habermacher, Maximilian Böhm, Sara Cerminara, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence promises democratized access to dermatological care, but model reliability depends on the quality and comprehensiveness of the underlying data. Despite rapid growth in publicly available dermatology images, the field lacks quantitative indicators to measure whether new datasets expand clinical coverage or merely replicate what is already known. Existing collections are widely assumed to be biased, yet the scale and topography of these gaps have remained unquantified, leaving the community without a road map for strategic data acquisition. Here, we show, by unifying 1.1 million images from 29 public datasets into a queryable semantic atlas, that the global archive is markedly skewed and increasingly redundant: darker skin tones (Fitzpatrick V–VI) constitute only 11.0% of images, pediatric patients only 2.3%, and informational novelty has plateaued despite exponential growth, revealing where targeted data acquisition is most needed.

Authors: Yifan Shen, Josey Hanish, Ishtiaque Ahmed Navid, Yuyang Pan, Zetian Mi, Theodore B. Norris
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Understanding carrier dynamics in semiconductor nanostructures is essential for optimizing their photocatalytic performance. We present direct optical evidence of ultrafast carrier separation in InGaN nanostructures used for water splitting. Two types of InGaN-based photocatalysts are studied: deepnano structures, which are a p-type InGaN micro-network, and nanowires incorporating an InGaN/GaN layered heterostructure. Here, we show that rapid lateral carrier separation in these nanostructures produces observable signatures in ultrafast spectroscopy. Using combined time-resolved photoluminescence and time-resolved differential reflectance spectroscopy, we observe photoluminescence exhibiting fast decay while differential reflection remains stable. This indicates rapid carrier separation. Studies of temperature and power-dependent photoluminescence confirm that carrier separation dominates over recombination-driven decay, and Mg doping studies reveal that stronger band bending enhances the carrier separation. The physical interpretation of the observations is supported by a numerical model including drift, diffusion, and thermal relaxation. The results provide critical insights into charge carrier dynamics in InGaN nanostructures, highlighting their potential for efficient photocatalysis.

Abstract: Abstract Nemaline myopathy is a rare congenital muscle disease associated with thin filament disruption that is currently without treatment. Biallelic mutations in Nebulin are the most common cause of nemaline myopathy. Nebulin encodes a giant protein with a primary function of establishing thin filament length. Nebulin protein has a large central region composed of a series of thin filament binding super repeats. Many Nebulin mutations are small in-frame deletions within individual super repeats. Why these deletions cause disease remains unclear. To study this, we generated a series of zebrafish lines, including ones carrying in-frame partial super repeat deletions and ones harboring complete/intact super repeat deletions. Partial super repeat deletions destabilize and reduce Nebulin protein, resulting in severe phenotypes and early death. Conversely, complete super repeat deletions preserve Nebulin stability and expression, and induce no overt phenotypes. Our work provides mechanistic insights and informs future therapeutic approaches for Nebulin-related Nemaline myopathy.

Abstract: Abstract Contemporary single-cell RNA-sequencing studies typically use RNA velocity analyses to investigate cellular dynamics. Commonly, RNA velocities are assessed with two-dimensional projections. Although it is well established that nonlinear embeddings of gene expression data cannot comprehensively preserve the structure of the original high-dimensional data across scales, there is no tool that systematically assesses and quantifies the faithfulness of velocity embeddings. This situation potentially leads to misleading velocity visualizations and putative cell state transitions. To this end, we introduce velotest, a cell-level statistical test that quantifies the faithfulness of a velocity embedding with respect to its high-dimensional counterpart. Applying velotest across multiple datasets and embedding methods, we find strong differences in the embedding qualities between embedding methods, datasets, and regions in individual datasets. velotest thus provides an essential validation step and enables researchers to select a suitable visualization of high-dimensional velocities, ensuring that hypotheses drawn from velocity projections are grounded in accurately represented dynamics.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Upon infection, arteriviruses, coronaviruses, and other nidoviruses transform endoplasmic reticulum membranes into viral replication organelles. These include large numbers of double-membrane vesicles (DMVs) whose interior is considered the primary site of viral RNA synthesis. Early studies characterized nidovirus DMVs as sealed compartments, leaving it unclear how newly synthesized viral RNA could be exported to the cytosol. The discovery of DMV-spanning pore complexes in coronavirus-infected cells provided a plausible solution for this topological challenge. However, their structural organization, functional features, and evolutionary conservation across the nidovirus order, have remained unclear. Here, we investigate the macromolecular architecture of DMVs induced by two prototypic arteriviruses using cellular cryo-electron tomography. Despite the substantial evolutionary distance separating arteriviruses and coronaviruses, we observe DMV-spanning pore complexes with striking structural similarities to those previously described in coronaviruses. These pores may facilitate both export and encapsidation of viral RNA. In the absence of viral RNA synthesis, ectopic expression of the arterivirus transmembrane nonstructural proteins nsp2 and nsp3 suffices to induce the formation of pore-containing DMVs. Together, our findings reveal the conservation of key structural features of DMV pores across two distantly related nidovirus families and support a central role for these pores in nidovirus replication.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11872
Abstract: Abstract C -glycosides are valuable compounds containing hydrolytically stable C-C bonds, yet their scarcity in nature and synthetic complexity limit their availability. Enzymes offer a sustainable route to C -glycosides, but few are known to display C -glycosylation activity and their mechanism remains unclear. Here, we study the intricacies of the maize C -glycosyltransferase Zm UGT708A6 using X-ray crystallography, biochemical assays, and atomistic simulations. Structural and dynamical analyses reveal two flexible gates that control substrate access and reactive conformations. Combined Quantum Mechanics/Molecular Mechanics simulations and mutational data support a stepwise S E Ar mechanism for C -glycosylation of neutral phloretin, mediated by the catalytic His-Asp dyad and involving a high-energy σ-complex that stabilizes through a water-mediated proton transfer. Complementary pH- and substrate-activity experiments, together with Quantum Mechanics calculations, indicate that substrate hydroxylation patterns, protonation states, and σ-complex energetics restrict the scope of C -glycosides. Our results provide a coherent mechanistic framework that reconciles experimental observations across diverse conditions and advances our understanding of enzymatic C -glycosylation.

item.title: A spectral framework for revealing the hidden low-dimensional structure in stochastic reaction networks
item.dc:creator: Ankit Gupta
Mustafa Khammash
item.description:
Authors: Ankit Gupta, Mustafa Khammash
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Stochastic reaction networks govern noise-driven dynamics in systems ranging from gene regulation to cellular signalling and population processes. Yet their high dimensionality and sensitivity to initial states obscure transient mechanisms and limit reliable inference from experimental data. Here, we show that stochastic reaction networks in biological systems often exhibit dominant low-dimensional spectral structure that shapes their dynamics. We develop a spectral framework based on the stochastic Koopman operator that identifies these dominant dynamical modes directly from simulated trajectories, yielding reduced representations with computable error bounds. This reduction enables accurate analytical descriptions of the time evolution of moments, parameter sensitivities, and cross-spectral densities, while achieving order-of-magnitude computational gains relative to standard simulation-based methods. Applied to synthetic gene circuits, our framework reveals the spectral organisation of stochastic oscillators, enables systematic comparison of competing intracellular controllers, and facilitates inference of initial-state distributions from single-cell snapshot population data collected over time. Together, these results establish a principled spectral description of stochastic reaction dynamics and provide a foundation for analysing and inferring high-dimensional noise-driven biological systems.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11877
Abstract: Abstract Given the large size of neurons, local maintenance of mitochondria is crucial to counteract insults to this organelle in axons and dendrites. The Parkinson-related mitochondrial kinase PINK1 plays a central role in mitochondrial quality control, which in neurons requires the transport of Pink1 mRNA by mitochondrial hitch-hiking. However, how and where PINK1 is locally translated and processed has remained unclear. Using live-cell imaging, we trace local PINK1 translation sites and preprotein dynamics, revealing a concerted interplay between mitochondria and the ER, with endolysosomes frequently localized adjacent to the site of translation. Upon metabolically regulated untethering from mitochondria, Pink1 mRNA relocates to ribosomes in proximity to the ER and endolysosomes for translation of the PINK1 preprotein. The ER chaperone DNAJB6 shields the PINK1 preprotein in transit to mitochondria, following the post-translational ER-SURF pathway. Consequently, loss of DNAJB6 leads to persistent ER/endolysosome-associated PINK1 precursor stores and failure of mitophagy upon mitochondrial damage. Our findings reveal that neuronal PINK1 protein translation switches between mitochondrially anchored co-translational and ER-associated post-translational import states, with functional implications for mitochondrial quality control.

Abstract: Abstract Anaerobic oxidation of methane (AOM) has been proposed as a source of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) at marine cold seeps, but the underlying molecular mechanism for its production remains unknown. Here we demonstrate a previously unrecognized link between AOM and porewater DOC by analyzing disaccharides in sediment and porewaters from a methane-charged cold seep in Astoria Canyon (Oregon, USA). Accordingly, disaccharides mediate a relationship that may sustain microbial food webs and influence carbon cycling in methane-rich marine sediments.

Abstract: Abstract Mineral dust affects atmospheric chemistry, air quality, and climate, yet its impacts remain uncertain because its mineral composition is poorly constrained. These results show that calcite variability strongly modulates heterogeneous chemistry, whereas iron oxides dominate radiative impacts.

Abstract: Abstract Adoptive T cell receptor (TCR)–based immunotherapy offers a powerful strategy to target solid tumors. However, how the physical properties of the antigen-presenting interface regulate T cell metabolic programming remains poorly defined. TCR-T cells expanded using fast-relaxing SynVAC-pMHC exhibit superior persistence and durable antitumor activity in melanoma and ovarian cancer models. These results establish cell-mimetic viscoelasticity as a key biophysical cue governing T cell metabolism and differentiation and offer a fully synthetic strategy for manufacturing potent TCR-T cells.

Abstract: Abstract Antihypertensive prescription is guided by cardiovascular risk prediction models. However, existing models often exclude individuals with prior cardiovascular disease or those prescribed statin treatment. Consequently, there is limited evidence regarding how the benefits and harms of treatment vary according to an individual’s baseline risk. This cohort study includes 5,578,002 patients aged≥40years (mean age 59; 52% women) from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink between 1998–2018. A cardiovascular risk prediction model is developed using the Clinical Practice Research Datalink GOLD dataset and externally validated using the Aurum dataset. The model demonstrates excellent calibration and discrimination. Antihypertensive therapy is more likely to prevent serious major cardiovascular events (eight events prevented per 1,000 patients over 10 years, 95% confidence interval = 1 to 14), than to cause serious falls (two events per 1,000 patients, 95% confidence interval = −4 to 10). The risks of other adverse events indicate more nuanced or potentially harmful trade-offs. Here we show that a cardiovascular risk prediction model developed using routinely collected primary care data accurately predicts risk across a broad population of patients eligible for antihypertensive treatment. These findings will enable clinicians to better communicate individualised benefits and risks of antihypertensive therapy.

Authors: Joonhee Won, Jaehyun Jang, Hyunseo Kim, Inyoung Choi, Kyunghyun Jo, Yunheum Lee, Jiheong Kang, Steve Park, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Skeletal muscles combine forceful contraction with built-in sensing of their own length and movement, known as proprioception. Reproducing this combination in soft artificial muscles remains difficult, because added sensors often reduce actuation performance, complicate fabrication or limit miniaturization. In natural muscle, specialized sensory fibers are embedded alongside, and mechanically coupled to, the force-generating fibers. Inspired by this arrangement, we pair a hyperelastic, highly stretchable fluid channel with a stiffer, off-center optical core inside a single thin fiber. When liquid is pumped in, the channel wall undergoes a shape bifurcation: a localized bulge forms and propagates along the fiber. Because the core resists stretching, the bulge bends the fiber into a contracting coil, while the core also reports the fiber’s shape through the light it transmits. Here we show that such fibers, produced continuously by a scalable drawing process, act as artificial muscles that sense their own contraction and stretching, supporting self-monitoring movement in soft robots.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Achieving sub-cellular resolution in ambient, matrix-free mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) remains challenging because reducing the sampling area often compromises ion yield and image fidelity. Here, we demonstrate an infrared laser–driven ambient MSI platform that mitigates these limitations through low-fluence, picosecond pulsed, high-repetition-rate laser ablation with a custom 2.94 μm light source with near-diffraction limited beam quality. This approach produces well-confined ablation features with diameters of 5 μm to 10 μm. Coupling the laser ablation plume to a rapid evaporative ionisation mass spectrometry (LA-REIMS) interface and a commercial time-of-flight mass analyser provides multiplexed ion maps of metabolites, phospholipids, and other small molecules in a single acquisition. This configuration enables routine 3 μm-pixel size imaging of fresh-frozen tissue sections, as well as imaging of formalin-fixed, paraffin embedded biopsy samples, all without additional preparation steps. Oversampled images preserve sub-cellular morphology and yield molecular distributions that correlate with fluorescence and histological features. Together, these results define a robust operational regime for high-fidelity, matrix-free MSI in the few- μ m pixel range, where high infrared beam quality and stable, low-fluence, high repetition rate picosecond laser sampling underpin gentle ablation and efficient ion formation via REIMS, enabling sub-cellular molecular mapping in a clinically compatible, fully ambient format.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11605
Abstract: Abstract Large language models may facilitate unlawful activities, yet this risk remains underexplored in studies assessing illicit-content recognition or narrow categories of illicit scenarios. We define complicit facilitation as model guidance that assists users with illicit instructions. To assess it, we develop a legally-informed, automated pipeline grounded in real-world cases and legal frameworks, and introduce EVIL, a benchmark covering 269 illicit scenarios and 50 illicit intents across Chinese and United States legal contexts. Evaluations indicate that complicit facilitation is widespread across models, with legal warnings and lawful alternatives often omitted. Risks vary across socio-legal contexts and are elevated for crimes against societal interests, non-violent offenses, and intents involving subjective motives or deceptive justifications. Models provide more complicit assistance when instructions describe users as older adults, racial minorities, non-religious individuals, or workers in lower-prestige occupations. Existing open-source safety benchmarks and alignment datasets offer limited coverage and mitigation of these risks.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract While 2- and 4-aryloxypyridines are ubiquitous in pharmaceutical molecules, efficient synthetic strategies—especially for synthesizing scaffolds with diverse multiple substituents on the pyridine core—remain limited. Here we show a hook-and-slide strategy for constructing these scaffolds, involving the in-situ generation of pyridonyl(aryl)iodonium salts from pyridones and Koser’s reagent (hook, C3 selectivity), followed by an iodine-to-oxygen aryl migration (slide, O selectivity). Such newly designed iodonium salts feature dual vicinal nucleophilic sites, and we demonstrate that using C2 − H imidazolium ionic liquids can exclusively transfer the aryl group to the strategic O site. This approach is transition-metal-free, scalable, and applicable to substrates with diverse electronic and steric properties or complex structures. Importantly, the resulting products retain −I and −NH 2 handles that are amenable to downstream derivatizations, enabling extensive exploration of previously inaccessible chemical space. The utility of this approach is further demonstrated through the concise synthesis of multiple pharmaceutical intermediates and a CRF 1 antagonist, CP-376395.

item.title: Evolutionary plasticity of bacterial surface layer protein exoskeletons
item.dc:creator: Anna Barwinska-Sendra
Paula S. Salgado
Kacper M. Sendra
item.description:
Authors: Anna Barwinska-Sendra, Paula S. Salgado, Kacper M. Sendra
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11797
Abstract: Abstract All cellular life possesses environmental interfaces like cell membranes or cell walls, yet the compositional complexity of these major cell components limits structural and evolutionary studies. Prokaryotic surface layer (S-layer) exoskeletons, with their homopolymer paracrystalline architecture, offer a more tractable model of an environmental interface. However, extreme sequence diversity and heterogeneous multidomain organisation of S-layer proteins confound conventional evolutionary analyses. Here, by combining phylogenomics with structural modelling, we show that extensive sequence divergence, modular evolution and lateral gene transfer drive lineage-specific S-layer diversification across both monoderm ( Bacillaceae , Peptostreptococcaceae ) and diderm ( Caulobacteraceae , Deinococcaceae ) bacteria. Focusing on the Gram-positive order Peptostreptococcales , including environmental isolates and clinical pathogens, we uncover multiple S-layer architectures conferring divergent physiological properties. Molecular microbiology reveals that among close relatives utilising the same exoskeleton type, only pathogens display resistance to the antimicrobial immune effectors LL-37 and lysozyme. Furthermore, by experimentally determining two S-layer structures, we unravel how mechanisms including (intra)domain gains and losses generate hyper-diversity of homologous S-layers among clinical isolates of the pathogen Clostridioides difficile . Our findings establish the S-layer as a paradigm of molecular modularity and evolutionary plasticity. Specifically, evolution of a single structural protein enables rapid cell-surface reconfiguration and contributes to immune evasion in bacterial pathogens.

item.title: Disturbance increases soil microbiome functional redundancy but decreases capacity for insurance via winnowed environmental responsiveness
item.dc:creator: Samuel E. Barnett
Ashley Shade
item.description:
Authors: Samuel E. Barnett, Ashley Shade
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Coexisting populations performing similar functions (i.e., functional redundancy), can stabilize ecosystem outputs under disturbance. The insurance hypothesis proposes that diversity maintains community function under disturbance because functionally redundant taxa differ in their environmental responsiveness. However, how redundancy and insurance interact in microbial communities remains unclear. Here, we examine functional redundancy and insurance potential in soil microbial communities under long-term heat disturbance from an underground coal seam fire in Centralia, Pennsylvania, USA, using seven years of deep metagenome sequencing across heated and reference sites. Functional redundancy increases with disturbance intensity, driven by declines in taxonomic diversity and average genome size and by increased per-genome investment in biogeochemically relevant metabolisms (i.e., carbohydrate and nitrogen). However, a proposed proxy for environmental responsiveness, transcription factor evenness, is reduced in heated soils. These results indicate that prolonged, selective disturbance can enhance redundancy while simultaneously constraining insurance against future stress, shaping microbial community resilience under persistent disturbance.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Phenylethanoid glycosides are structurally diverse natural products widely found in traditional medicinal plants and display a broad range of biological activities. However, systematic studies of their functions and structure–activity relationships have been limited by inefficient access to diverse analogs in useful quantities. Here we show a protecting-group-lean synthetic platform that provides a 29-member library of phenylethanoid glycosides with variations at four positions of the central glucose unit. The strategy combines regioselective glycosylation, β-selective glycosylation without neighboring-group assistance, selective caffeoylation, and a mild global deprotection that preserves labile caffeoyl esters. Two glycosylations and two additional transformations can be performed sequentially in one pot, substantially streamlining assembly. Biological evaluation in a TGF-β-induced fibroblast model reveals structure–activity relationships, provides insight into signaling pathways associated with antifibrotic activity, and identifies several compounds as promising leads for further antifibrotic studies.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11833
Abstract: Abstract The parasite Trypanosoma brucei lives in the body fluids of its hosts, including blood and interstitial fluids of various tissues. The mechanism of dissemination within these environments remains largely unresolved, although the trypanosome´s motility is known to play an essential role for its survival. The unicellular flagellate is a versatile microswimmer, like bacteria or sperm cells, albeit structurally more complex than these classical models. Here we study their motility in different viscous and elastic regimes. Using quantitative high speed video microscopy and digital holography microscopy, we detail the three-dimensional mechanical reaction of the flexible cell body with its uniquely attached flagellum to increasing confinement, leading to a network-threading type propulsion. This allows stable progressive motility despite a reduction in wave parameters up to tissue-like confinement. We thus show how trypanosomes can mechanically adjust in response to various microenvironments and, using flagellar beat reversal, manage the exploration of their complex environments.

item.dc:creator: Amy Heshmati

item.description:
Authors: Amy Heshmati, Sol P. Juárez
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11639
Abstract: Abstract Mental health conditions in the postpartum period are common. Generous parental leave has been shown to protect against poorer postpartum mental health among mothers; however, evidence for fathers remains limited. We examine whether levels of paid parental leave benefits are associated with fathers’ mental health in the first year after childbirth in Sweden. Using national population registers, we include 210,285 first-time fathers whose children were born between 2007 and 2011. Fathers receiving basic benefits have higher odds of receiving any mental healthcare, being prescribed antidepressants or anxiolytics, and using specialist outpatient care than those receiving higher-level earnings-related benefits. The results are robust after adjusting for mental health history, income and employment status, though associations are attenuated. Fathers who do not take parental leave during the first year are more likely to receive any mental healthcare, specialist outpatient care or hospitalisation. Overall, fathers with access to more generous paid parental leave benefits experience better postpartum mental health. These findings suggest that well-compensated parental leave may benefit fathers’ mental health and promote gender equality in caregiving. However, further efforts are needed to determine whether parental leave systems mitigate or reproduce health inequalities given that parental leave benefit levels are contingent on labour market conditions.

Abstract: Abstract Chiral molecules interact with light so weakly that discriminating enantiomers or driving enantioselective chemistry by using optical approaches requires intense circularly polarised lasers or complex resonant structures. Here we combine a geometrically disordered electrodeposited network with a lithographic chiral template resembling the shape of a shuriken. The resulting substrate generates superchiral fields that neither individual component produces. This chiral plasmonic nanoporous network achieves not only ultrasensitive chiral detection by reaching the attomole range, but also introduces enantiospecific photochemical reactivity on a single substrate under continuous-wave linearly polarised light. Raman asymmetries approach the theoretical maximum ( ≈ 2), while enantiomeric excesses exceed 25%. Finally, a six-order-of-magnitude enhancement over conventional Raman optical activity was calculated.

Abstract: Abstract A new generation of medications for obesity could transform the global food system. Abstract: Abstract The oxidative dehydrogenation of propane offers a promising route to propylene, but developing low-temperature catalysts that simultaneously achieve high activity and selectivity remains a formidable challenge. Here, we report a Co@BO x inverse catalyst featuring engineered defects localized at face-centered cubic/hexagonal close-packed phase boundaries within the subsurface cobalt promoter. Using an oxidative atmosphere-induced exsolution strategy, we continuously tune the face-centered cubic/hexagonal close-packed phase ratio, maximizing the density of stacking faults at a 1:1 phase ratio. Density functional theory reveals that stacking faults modulate Co atomic spacing, weakening the excessively strong BO x -Co interfacial interaction. In situ spectroscopy demonstrates that maximized stacking faults strengthen O-H bonds in surface boron hydroxyl species and optimize radical initiation kinetics. This work establishes subsurface defect engineering as a potential strategy to enhance oxide overlayer reactivity in inverse catalytic systems.

Abstract: Abstract Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy provides unparalleled access to molecular structure and dynamics but is traditionally limited by weak signal strength, requiring large sample volumes and high magnetic fields. Temperature-dependent measurements of a deuterated polymer and a molecular solid reveal distinct motional averaging and phase transitions with nanoscale sensitivity. Powder-like NV-detected 2 H NMR establishes a powerful tool for probing molecular dynamics on the nanoscale - capabilities beyond those of most existing spectroscopic techniques.

Authors: Vladimir Farenkov, Mengfan Guo, Jiaqi Zhang, Melony Dilshad, Nadia A. Stelmashenko, Xavier Moya, Sakyo Hirose, Neil D. Mathur
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Multilayer capacitors of PbSc 0.5 Ta 0.5 O 3 with good B-site cation order ( S 111 ~ 0.9-0.96) are driven by supercritical fields of 15.8 V μm −1 in prototype coolers, such that large electrocaloric effects arise over a wide range of temperatures and peak to give thermocouple-measured temperature jumps of |∆ T j | ~ 4.0 K near room temperature. However, the high degree of B-site order requires an energetically expensive 42-day high-temperature anneal that would be economically expensive and environmentally damaging in mass production. Here we report that the performance reduction (4.0 K → 3.1 K) for unannealed multilayer capacitors of PbSc 0.5 Ta 0.5 O 3 with partial B-site order ( S 111 ~ 0.6) is surprisingly small because reduced latent heat is mitigated by high-field electrocaloric effects in the induced ferroelectric phase. Eliminating the anneal without unduly compromising performance should render unannealed multilayer capacitors of PbSc 0.5 Ta 0.5 O 3 attractive for applications.
